The wrong pair is (1) Kavasaji Davar – Iron and Steel factory.

The chapter says that Kawasjee Dawar started the first textile mill in Mumbai in 1854. He is connected with the textile mill, not with an iron and steel factory.

The other three pairs are correct. Dr Datta Samant was asked by the workers to accept their leadership and he led the strike of the workers of 65 mills. Narayan Meghaji Lokhande's efforts resulted in the weekly Sunday holiday for mill workers from 1st January 1882. Narayan Surve was one of the poets who portrayed the real life of the workers through his poems.

| Five-year plan | Duration | Purposes |
|---|---|---|
| First | 1951-1956 | Agriculture, Social development |
| Second | 1956-1961 | Industrialisation |
| Third | 1961-1966 | Elimination of inequality, increasing the opportunities for employment, increase in national income |
| Fourth | 1969-1974 | Scientific research, health and family planning |
| Fifth | 1974-1979 | Alleviation of poverty and making India economically self-sufficient; increase in the national income; large scale employment; supply of education, nutritious food and drinking water; medical facilities in rural areas; development of agriculture and basic industries; supply of food grains to the poor at reasonable prices through the public distribution system |

[Note: the chapter does not describe the Fourth Five Year Plan (1969-1974) in terms of scientific research, health and family planning as the printed chart does. The chapter states that the aims of the Fourth Plan were that India should become self-reliant, that the government should develop the basic industries, increase the speed of economic development and pay attention to establishing a socialistic pattern of society, and that 14 major banks were nationalised during this plan. Only the plan name has been filled in from the duration 1969-1974 given in the chart.]

A mixed economy is an economy that works both in the private sector and in the public sector. Before independence some countries had adopted capitalism, in which the means of production are privately owned, and some had adopted socialism, in which the means of production are owned by the State in the name of the society. Prime Minister Pandit Nehru did not go to either extreme but adopted the middle path, and India gave preference to the model of a mixed economy for the economic development of modern India.

This economy has three parts. In the public sector the industries are completely under the control and management of the government, for example the production of defence equipment. In the private sector the industries are owned by private industrialists, though the government supervises and controls them too, for example consumer goods. In the joint sector some industries are owned by private industrialists while some are run under government management.

A mixed economy needs coordination between the private and the public sector. It aims at maximisation of production and popular participation on a large scale, and it tries to bring together the good aspects of both the capitalist and the socialist systems.

Prime Minister Indira Gandhi announced the 20-point programme on 1st July 1975. Through it she resolved to make efforts towards rapidly becoming a developed nation.

The main provisions of the programme were land ceiling for cities and agricultural land, equal division of wealth, minimum wages for workers and an increase in water conservation schemes. It also provided for workers' participation in industry, a national training scheme and the freeing of bonded labour. Another provision was the prevention of tax evasion, economic crimes and smuggling. The programme also included regulation of the prices of basic necessities and improvements in the public distribution system. Finally, it provided for improvement in the textile industry by developing the handloom sector, waiving loans for weaker sections, housing, communication facilities and making educational equipment available to schools.

Independent India opted for a mixed economy because Prime Minister Pandit Nehru chose the middle path instead of taking recourse to either extreme of capitalism or socialism, as each type of economy had its own advantages. A mixed economy works both in the private and the public sector, so an effort could be made through it to bring together the good aspects of both the capitalist and the socialist systems.

It also suited the needs of a newly independent country. A mixed economy naturally gives priority to national interest and stresses long term development. Industries like defence, scientific research, education, roads, railways, waterways, sea port and airport development require huge capital investment but the returns in these areas are delayed, so not many private industrialists are keen to invest in them; in such a situation the government has to take the initiative. At the same time the system does not ignore the profit motive, entrepreneurship, discipline and time bound planning, and it aims at maximisation of production and popular participation on a large scale. For these reasons India adopted the mixed economy model along with five year plans and started off on its path of development.

During the tenure of Prime Ministers Pandit Nehru and Lal Bahadur Shastri, banking was a monopoly of the private sector. These banks represented different industrial groups and their Directors were working towards developing the industrial sector and increasing its profits. Nationalisation was needed to stop this.

India had adopted a mixed economy after independence, and nationalisation of banks was essential to cover the deficits if they occurred while implementing different schemes. Once the banks were nationalised their profits would also come into the government treasury. Along with this, the policy of developing small industries and pharmaceutical industries had to be implemented, and Lal Bahadur Shastri had undertaken the experiment of the Green Revolution to overcome food shortages and drought, which needed the support of the banks.

During the tenure of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, the 'Congress Forum for Socialist Action', a group in the Congress party inspired by socialist ideas, demanded the nationalisation of commercial banks, and even the Communist Party supported this demand. For all these reasons Prime Minister Indira Gandhi nationalised 14 banks on 19th July 1969.

In the 1980s there was increasing unrest among the workers because of the economic conditions in other sectors. In some industries the wages of the workers were increasing and they were also getting larger amounts as bonus and more facilities than the textile mill workers were getting.

The immediate reason was the cut in the bonus. In the Diwali of 1981 the workers expected to get a bonus of 20 per cent, but the Rashtriya Mill Mazdoor Sangh, which was negotiating with the employers, agreed upon a bonus of 8 to 17 per cent without taking the workers into confidence. This cut in the bonus proved to be the cause of the unrest.

Some workers therefore went to Dr Datta Samant and asked him to accept their leadership. Workers of 65 mills came together and Dr Datta Samant led the strike. On 18th January 1982, two and a half lakh workers went on strike and the Girangaon mills stopped running.

The Eighth Five Year Plan covered the period 1992-1997 and gave a lot of scope to the private sector.

The following programmes were started during this plan:

1. Pradhanmantri Rozgar Yojana
2. Mahila Samriddhi Yojana
3. Rashtriya Samajik, Arthik Sahayya Yojana
4. Midday Meal Scheme
5. Indira Mahila Scheme
6. Ganga Kalyan Scheme

The features of the plan were to maintain the rate of growth in national income at 6.5 per cent, to control the growth of population, to encourage the programme of family planning and to remove illiteracy by the expansion of primary education. During the eighth plan the importance of the private sector grew. This plan is a reflection of the liberalisation and free market policy adopted in 1991.

The Second Five Year Plan covered the period 1956-1961 and had ambitious goals of industrialisation. Many heavy industries were set up in the public sector under this plan.

The following projects were started:

1. Iron and steel industries at Durgapur, Bhilai and Rourkela
2. Chemical fertilisers plant at Sindri
3. Rail engine factory at Chittaranjan
4. Factory of railway bogies at Perambur
5. Ship building factory at Vishakhapattanam

Besides these, huge dams like Bhakra-Nangal and Damodar were built to make water available for agriculture. All these projects led to an increase in the national income.
